title: ⭐⭐ Practice: orders, opinions and the words that judge

questions.prompt: Two adjectives of the lesson look interchangeable and are not. Wassim never tells a lie: when he broke the club's window he said so before anybody asked. But he has missed three of the last four meetings, and twice he simply forgot them. Which sentence weighs him correctly?

options.text: He is reliable, but he is not truthful.
He is neither truthful nor reliable.
He is truthful, but he is not reliable.
He is both truthful and reliable.

questions.explanation: "He is truthful, but he is not reliable." is the right weighing: truthful judges what a person says about what happened, and Wassim accused himself before anybody asked; reliable judges the distance between what a person promised and what they did, and three missed meetings out of four close that question. "He is reliable, but he is not truthful." turns the two adjectives round and calls a man reliable on the strength of the very meetings he missed. "He is neither truthful nor reliable." throws away the window he owned up to, which is exactly the evidence for the first adjective. And "He is both truthful and reliable." is the mistake the lesson is built to prevent: it treats the two words as one, when a person can be perfectly honest and still forget every appointment.

questions.prompt: Nizar writes the same fact twice. In the composition he hands to his English teacher: "The bridge was closed for repairs. ___, the buses went round by the old road." On the telephone to his cousin: "They shut the bridge — ___ the buses went round by the old road." Which pair fills the two gaps in the register each one needs?

options.text: therefore ... that's why
that's why ... therefore
therefore ... therefore
that's why ... that's why

questions.explanation: "therefore ... that's why" is the pair. The two linkers name the same relation, cause and result, but they do not live in the same places: "therefore" belongs to careful written English — a composition, a report, an examination paper — while "that's why" carries a contraction and belongs to speech and to friendly writing. The first gap settles the matter twice over, because a comma follows it: therefore takes that comma, and that's why never does. "that's why ... therefore" gets both halves wrong at once, putting the spoken form into the composition and the written form into a telephone call. "therefore ... therefore" makes a boy talking to his cousin sound as though he were reading a document aloud. And "that's why ... that's why" costs the composition the level of language a teacher expects from it.

questions.prompt: Mouna is the captain of the school handball team. Nobody ever stays behind to put the equipment away, and she wants to say that she too must stay, not only the others. Which line does she use?

options.text: Stay ten minutes after the match.
You must stay ten minutes after the match.
Don't leave as soon as the match ends.
Let's stay ten minutes after the match.

questions.explanation: "Let's stay ten minutes after the match." is the line: let's is short for let us, and it is the only imperative that puts the speaker inside the order she is giving. "Stay ten minutes after the match." is a bare imperative, and a bare imperative is addressed to the people in front of the speaker, never to the speaker herself. "You must stay ten minutes after the match." leaves her out twice over — the subject you names the others, and must turns the sentence into a rule imposed from above. And "Don't leave as soon as the match ends." forbids something instead of proposing it, and it too speaks only to the others.

questions.prompt: Two teachers say exactly the same words to Nizar: "You handed in your project yesterday, didn't you?" The first lets her voice fall at the end; the second lets her voice rise. What does the rising voice tell Nizar?

options.text: She already knows he handed it in and simply wants him to say yes.
She does not know whether he handed it in and is really asking.
She is telling him to hand in his project today.
She is correcting a mistake he made in the project.

questions.explanation: "She does not know whether he handed it in and is really asking." is right: with the same words, a rising voice on the tag turns the sentence into a genuine question, because the speaker has no idea what the answer will be. "She already knows he handed it in and simply wants him to say yes." describes the other teacher, the one whose voice falls: a falling tag asks only for confirmation of something already believed. "She is telling him to hand in his project today." reads the sentence as an order, but an order has no subject and no tag of this kind. And "She is correcting a mistake he made in the project." invents a content the words do not carry: the tag says nothing about the quality of the work, only about the speaker's certainty.

questions.prompt: Your class is debating what money does to people. A speaker has to open with an opinion of their own, not with a fact anybody can check. Which of these four lines is an opinion?

options.text: Money spoils a friendship before anybody admits it.
Our class collected forty dinars for the library.
The school opened its new library in September.
Two of the four bakeries in our town closed last year.

questions.explanation: "Money spoils a friendship before anybody admits it." is the opinion: it is a judgement, and another speaker may stand up and refuse it without proving anything wrong — which is exactly what makes a debate possible. "Our class collected forty dinars for the library." states a sum, and a sum is checked, not discussed. "The school opened its new library in September." states a date, which is checked in the same way. And "Two of the four bakeries in our town closed last year." states a number of events; a speaker may build an opinion on top of it, but the line itself only reports what happened.

questions.prompt: Rania is preparing a paragraph for the class debate on money. One of her four sentences has to be crossed out: it is perfectly true, but it does nothing for the point she is making. "(1) A family that cannot pay for school books loses more than money: it loses choices. (2) I have seen a good student leave in March because his father needed him at the market. (3) The market of our town is open every day except Friday afternoon. (4) Poverty does not make a man dishonest, but it takes half of his answers away." Which sentence goes?

options.text: the family that loses its choices
the student who left in March
the opening days of the market
poverty and a man's answers

questions.explanation: "the opening days of the market" is the sentence to cross out, the third one: the timetable of a market is a fact anybody can check, but Rania is arguing that poverty takes choices away, and the days a market opens on prove nothing at all about that. "the family that loses its choices" states the very idea the paragraph defends, so it is the one sentence that could never go. "the student who left in March" is the example that carries the idea into real life, and an argument without an example convinces nobody. And "poverty and a man's answers" closes the paragraph by saying how far the writer is willing to go, which is where a debate speaker has to end.
